analysis.one_liner: Lets employers skip overtime pay for hours employees worked without permission.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal overtime law so that an employer would not have to pay time-and-a-half for any hours over 40 in a week unless the employer had authorized those hours in advance. It was introduced by one representative, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, referred to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who ask or allow employees to work long hours. Under the bill, any overtime hours worked without the employer's sign-off would become unpaid, shifting the cost of that work from the employer to the worker.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to say an employer 'shall not be required to pay' overtime compensation for hours over 40 in a workweek if those hours were worked without the employer's authorization.
The change would have taken effect 180 days after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Hourly workers covered by the overtime law. Hours they put in beyond 40 a week without written or prior employer approval would become unpaid, so the employee absorbs the cost of extra work.

drawbacks.text: Workers often work extra hours because a supervisor tells them to or because the job demands it; a blanket rule that unauthorized overtime is unpaid would put workers at risk of doing required work without pay, and disputes over what counts as 'authorization' would fall hardest on the employee.
The bill would weaken the enforcement structure of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which currently requires overtime pay for all covered hours over 40 regardless of whether the employer approved them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs almost entirely to employers, who would gain a way to avoid time-and-a-half pay; the cost falls on the workers whose extra hours would go unpaid. Because it never advanced, no one actually gained or lost under it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee on labor standards, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Ramstad introduced the bill on June 25, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On August 13, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had no cosponsors at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hourly workers are better off, since the existing overtime guarantee stays intact. The bill's sponsor and supportive employers gained nothing, but the proposal could be reintroduced in a later Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hourly workers who keep overtime protections

for.name: Rep. Jim Ramstad
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt employers from paying overtime for unauthorized hours worked.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to a subcommittee; took no further action, so the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so there is no record of a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have let employers avoid time-and-a-half pay for any overtime hours not explicitly authorized, transferring that cost to employees. It never advanced, so employers gained nothing.
